subject: Climate & Environment
title: Soil: The Hidden Forest
description: A 60-second lesson on Soil: The Hidden Forest.

hook.text: The forest beneath your feet holds more life than the canopy above your head.

buildup.text: One tablespoon of forest soil contains more microorganisms than people on Earth.

discovery.text: Fungi form underground networks connecting trees — sharing nutrients and chemical warnings.

twist.text: Scientists call it the 'wood wide web.' Mother trees feed their seedlings through it.

climax.text: Forest soil stores 45% of all terrestrial carbon — more than the trees themselves.

punchline.text: The real forest is underground. The trees are just the visible part.

quiz.question: What percentage of terrestrial carbon is stored in forest soil?

details.summary: Forest soils contain more carbon than all the trees above them combined, along with vast fungal networks, bacteria, and invertebrates that drive nutrient cycling. When forests are cleared, soil carbon oxidizes and erodes, releasing centuries of stored carbon within years.
details.whyItMatters: Soil is the largest terrestrial carbon pool and the foundation of forest productivity. Ignoring soil in deforestation accounting vastly underestimates the true carbon loss.
takeaways: Forest soils store roughly twice as much carbon as aboveground biomass
Mycorrhizal fungi connect trees in nutrient-sharing networks
Soil erosion after clearing can remove the fertile layer within decades

faq.question: What is the wood wide web?
faq.answer: It refers to underground mycorrhizal fungal networks that connect tree roots, allowing them to share water, nutrients, and chemical signals. These networks help young trees survive and allow forests to function as interconnected organisms.

faq.question: How quickly is soil carbon lost after deforestation?
faq.answer: Soil carbon loss begins immediately as exposure to sun and rain accelerates decomposition and erosion. Studies show 20 to 40 percent of topsoil carbon can be lost within the first decade after tropical forest clearing.
